messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amina is a 35-year-old tutor who came to treatment months after being raped, an assault that happened after an evening lesson when she was walking to her car through a residential block. What has remained most vivid is not a clear spoken story she can tell from beginning to end, but fragments that still seize her body: the sound of a child crying somewhere nearby from an upstairs apartment, the sharp roll of nausea as fear rose in her throat, and the terrible uncertainty of not knowing what the man was going to do next. Even now, when she tries to describe the attack, she stops and says it feels as if she is talking about something that happened to another woman. The memory does not come as a narrative she can hold at a distance; it arrives with the same terror, wordless and immediate, and that strangeness has helped convince her that something in her has been permanently altered for the worse.

In the weeks after the rape, Amina found that the things that pulled her back toward the assault were oddly specific and difficult to explain to people around her. A child crying in the hallway of the building where she tutors, or outside a family’s front door as she waits for a student, can make her stomach turn instantly. Moments of uncertainty are just as potent: a late text from a parent changing a lesson time, an unfamiliar voice in a house, not knowing who else is home. The sensation of nausea itself has become a warning sign she dreads. Each time one of these moments hits, she has come to believe it proves how fragile she now is. If a crying child or a brief spell of not knowing what to expect can undo her so quickly, then in her mind it means she cannot handle even the slightest upset.

Because she is so certain that thinking about the rape will overwhelm her, Amina has organized her days around not giving it room. She repeatedly blames herself in long, punishing loops—rehearsing what she wore, why she stayed late, whether she should have noticed danger sooner—as if finding the mistake might make the event containable. She also steers away from anything that might make her feel happy or hopeful, declining outings with her partner and brushing off small celebrations after good teaching days because the lightness feels unsafe and undeserved. When friends or family edge toward asking what happened, she changes the subject or leaves. These habits make sense to her as protection; she believes that if she lets herself think directly about the assault, or lets herself feel too much of anything, she will lose control.

Yet the way she avoids has left the memory even less speakable. The more she cuts off conversations and turns from reminders, the less the experience feels like something she can place in words. Instead it stays in disconnected pieces that rush back with full terror. After nights spent mentally circling self-blaming questions, she often wakes already tense and nauseated, and ordinary uncertainty the next day feels charged before anything has happened. In tutoring sessions she has become acutely alert to sounds in the home, especially children crying in another room, and she reads her own bodily reaction as further evidence that she is damaged beyond repair. Avoiding hopeful moments has narrowed her life with her partner; he has begun to describe her as absent even when she is beside him, and she privately fears he is seeing the ruined version of her that she feels she has become.

At work, this has become concrete. Amina used to enjoy traveling between students’ homes and adapting easily to family routines. Now she asks for as much information as possible in advance and feels panicked when plans are uncertain. If she hears a child crying as she arrives, she sometimes sits in her car until the lesson start time, fighting nausea and trying not to think. If a parent casually mentions a neighborhood incident or asks a question that brushes against safety, she becomes quiet and shut down for the rest of the session. Afterwards she may spend hours blaming herself for reacting, which only deepens her conviction that she cannot cope.

By the time she sought help, Amina felt trapped by the very measures she had been using to get through. The memories were still alien and unsayable, the triggers were multiplying, and every effort to avoid being overwhelmed seemed to leave her more easily undone. She came because she is frightened that this is permanent—that a child crying, a wave of nausea, or any moment of uncertainty will always be enough to bring the terror back—and because, despite that fear, part of her still hopes there might be a way to remember what happened without disappearing into it.
